channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Textile electrodes could bring wearable relief for menstrual pain and muscle soreness
item.description: Applying a mild electrical current through the skin is a drug-free way to manage menstrual pain and intense muscle soreness, but at-home devices that deliver the current are bulky and difficult to use effectively, and they require sticky gels. Now, scientists reporting in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces have developed a reusable pain-relieving textile electrode that could be incorporated into clothing. In a preliminary test, the electrodes transmitted electrical stimulation through skin-care products to a person's skin.

item.title: Counting gut bacteria sheds new light on multiple sclerosis
item.description: Researchers from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), Flemish Institute for Biotechnology, KU Leuven and the Belgian National MS Centre in Melsbroek have taken a significant step toward understanding the relationship between gut microbiota and multiple sclerosis (MS). This could lead to better insights and treatments in the future.

item.title: Growing miniature tumors to help personalize cancer treatment
item.description: Modern cancer care is based on many factors. Physicians use scans, lab tests and decades of clinical research to help decide which treatments are best for patients.

item.title: How persistent inflammation reprograms the immune system to promote T-cell exhaustion
item.description: When the body encounters an infection, its immune system must respond rapidly and effectively. Dendritic cells play a central role in this process. They detect pathogens, capture their components and activate specialized immune cells known as CD8 T cells, which can recognize and eliminate infected cells.

item.title: E-scooter injuries can cause lasting symptoms and work disruption
item.description: Many people treated for traumatic brain injury (TBI) after electric scooter crashes experience significant time away from work and symptoms that persist for months, according to findings published Nov. 17 in JAMA Network Open.

item.title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally. Social media, celebrities reduce taboos and influence beauty ideals
item.description: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

item.title: Sleeping 9 or more hours linked to a higher risk of death in people with heart disease
item.description: Adults with heart disease who sleep nine or more hours a day may be at greater risk of dying prematurely. That's the conclusion of a study published in the journal PLOS One that examined the relationship between sleep duration and mortality in more than 3,000 adults from the U.S.

item.title: The DRC's Ebola crisis revives an old ethical question: What do health workers owe patients?
item.description: The World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026. As of Nov. 18, there have been 11,712 cases and 5,720 deaths, nearly all in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC.

item.title: Pimple‑popping videos can be disgusting—and strangely satisfying
item.description: Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger's face. I'm one of them. I have favorite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

item.title: What if rheumatoid arthritis could be prevented before the pain begins?
item.description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) begins years before someone experiences the joint pain, swelling and stiffness associated with the disease. Now, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz are exploring how artificial intelligence and advances in biological research could help identify the immune mechanisms underlying those early warning symptoms and signs and potentially prevent the disease before it starts.

item.title: Glucose sensors for type 2 diabetes deserve second look from NHS
item.description: A wearable sensor that allows people with type 2 diabetes using insulin to track their glucose levels in real time could prove good value for the NHS, a University of Manchester–led study suggests. The research, published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, assessed the value for money of real-time continuous glucose monitoring compared with standard finger-prick testing.

item.title: Summer may be best time to test for vitamin D deficiency
item.description: Swedish women and men with low vitamin D levels when tested in the summer had a higher risk of bone fractures and death—risks not seen in people with low test results during winter.

item.title: Exploring the underrecognized role of lipid metabolism in neurodegenerative disease
item.description: Ole Isacson, M.D., Ph.D., founding director of the Neuroregeneration Institute at McLean Hospital within Mass General Brigham, is the lead and corresponding author of a paper published in Cell Reports Medicine titled "Lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism in neurodegenerative disease: a maturing framework to guide therapeutic development," co-authored with Penelope Hallett, Ph.D. Their perspective article supports a broader interpretation of neurodegenerative disease in which lipid metabolism, cellular energy regulation, inflammation and protein abnormalities form an interconnected biological system.

item.title: Researchers look beyond the screen to help keep seniors, people with cognitive concerns connected
item.description: Nancy Roderer '73's online physical therapy sessions are an important part of her routine, so she initially brushed off a recent stumble she took while logged on alone at home.

item.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding bone disease with 'catastrophic' impact on new moms may be missed by doctors
item.description: An in-depth study of women with pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis (PLO), a rare condition affecting around 50 women a year in the U.K., found it causes debilitating multiple fractures, acute and chronic pain, disability and long-term psychological distress. The research was carried out by Imperial College London, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Trust and is published in Osteoporosis International.

item.title: Paxlovid tied to 12% lower risk of long COVID in high-risk adults
item.description: Adults at high risk for severe COVID-19 who were prescribed nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) within five days of infection were less likely to be hospitalized or die in the next six months than those who weren't given the antiviral drug, according to a large study published in PLOS Global Public Health. For patients at low risk for severe outcomes, the results were inconclusive.

item.title: Flu vaccine might help stave off early signs of Alzheimer's
item.description: Brain health is a concern for many older adults because it's tied to their longevity and independence. A new study published in the Annals of Geriatric Medicine and Research finds that getting the flu shot might help people stay sharp, as vaccinated adults were less likely to experience signs of dementia.

item.title: Straight to the source: The case for targeted immunotherapy for lupus
item.description: CAR T-cell therapy is an established treatment for some blood cancers, engineering a person's own T cells to recognize and attack specific cell types, including cancer cells. In recent years, CAR-T therapy has been shown to also work for conditions beyond cancer.

item.title: Researchers develop a novel scaffold HPK1 inhibitor for cancer immunotherapy
item.description: Scientists have recently developed IHMT-HPK1-550, a small-molecule HPK1 inhibitor featuring a novel scaffold, providing a new candidate compound for cancer immunotherapy. The study was led by professor Liu Qingsong from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the findings were published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry on Oct. 28.

item.title: Two new studies point to advances in personalized lung cancer treatment
item.description: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States, but for a growing number of patients, the outlook is improving. As Lung Cancer Awareness Month draws attention to the disease and advances in care, Marina Garassino, M.D., a thoracic oncologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, is helping push the field forward.

item.title: Mail-order antibiotic kits pose safety, resistance risks, pharmacy expert warns
item.description: Sometimes, inspiration can spark from interesting places.

item.title: An unexpected link: More coarse particles in indoor air, lower odds of Kawasaki disease
item.description: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute inflammatory condition that primarily affects children under 5. It causes inflammation of blood vessels throughout the body and can lead to serious complications, particularly affecting the coronary arteries that supply blood to the heart. Although Kawasaki disease is a major cause of acquired heart disease in children, its exact cause remains unclear. Genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures are thought to contribute to its development, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood.

item.title: Norovirus is spreading—how to recognize the symptoms and what to do
item.description: Described as the "Ferrari of the virus world" for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

item.title: Large clinical trial clarifies clot prevention trade-offs after hip and knee replacement
item.description: A large, multisite clinical trial involving researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) has provided important new evidence about the medications commonly used to prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots following hip and knee replacement surgery.

item.title: Blood tests and new cancer models reveal how small cell lung cancer responds to and resists tarlatamab
item.description: Researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have used a blood-based test combined with the development of new preclinical models to follow how small cell lung cancer responds to tarlatamab and changes as it becomes resistant. The study identified a tumor subtype associated with greater treatment benefit and revealed two ways the cancer may escape therapy.

item.title: Brain lesions: What causes them and when they need follow‑up
item.description: You open your brain scan report and see the word "lesion." It's a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor. In a report, it means there's an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that's been there for years.

item.title: Programming cancer immunity with 3 mRNAs: Development of a modular mRNA cocktail
item.description: A research team has developed a modular mRNA cocktail that combines three types of mRNA encoding a tumor antigen, a costimulatory molecule and a cytokine, and successfully demonstrated its ability to synergistically activate T cells specific for cancer antigens. The research is published in the journal OncoImmunology.

item.title: A new drug treatment for head and neck cancer
item.description: On Nov. 5, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the use of a new drug to treat head and neck cancer, the first in seven years. Called amivantamab, the drug is the first to target two growth receptors for head and neck cancer simultaneously, reducing the cancer's ability to adapt to the treatment. The FDA granted amivantamab accelerated approval because of the promising results it showed during clinical trials, which were led by Yale School of Medicine researchers.

item.title: Hot nights linked to poorer memory in middle-aged and older Australians
item.description: As overnight temperatures continue to rise across Australia, a new study suggests warmer nights may be linked to poorer memory in middle-aged and older Australians.

item.title: Inhaled antibiotics may enhance immunotherapy by targeting bacteria in lung metastases
item.description: Researchers at the Leibniz Institute for Immunotherapy (LIT) in Regensburg, Germany, at the University of Milan and at the National Cancer Institute (INT) in Milan, Italy, have identified tumor-associated bacteria in lung metastases as a potential barrier to immunotherapy. In mice, aerosolized antibiotics disrupted this immunosuppressive environment and enhanced treatment responses, including complete tumor regressions. The study is published in Cancer Immunology Research.
